idiom_name: Task.Run fan-out + Task.WhenAll join on the shared ThreadPool (TPL)
implementation_notes: The .NET master is an async method: Task.Run (or Parallel.For/ForEach for blocking CPU partitions) fans the sub-tasks out onto the shared ThreadPool and Task.WhenAll is the join, returning the partial results in input order - the TPL already performs partitioning, scheduling and continuation, so no role objects are written. Task.WhenAll aggregates every fault into a single AggregateException and lets the remaining tasks finish, while awaiting tasks one by one stops at the first failure; choose deliberately and decide whether partial results count. Never block a pool thread on Task.Result or Wait() (sync-over-async): it starves the shared pool and can deadlock. Cap concurrency with ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism or a Parallel.ForEachAsync loop when the fan-out is large.
pitfalls: Sync-over-async (.Result/.Wait()) holds a pool thread while waiting: with enough fan-out the shared ThreadPool starves and the join deadlocks.
Task.WhenAll surfaces failures as an AggregateException, and canceling the combined task does not stop the individual tasks - decide whether a failed partial discards the batch or is retried.

The ThreadPool is shared with the rest of the application (and with Parallel.For): nested parallel regions or thousands of Task.Run calls oversubscribe it, so bound the degree of parallelism explicitly.
Closures over mutable state captured by Task.Run race: the tasks may start after the loop variable or the accumulator was mutated.
